title: A Story of Numbers
subject: Maths-1
description: How humans learned to count and write numbers — from tally marks and Gumulgal twos through Roman, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Mayan and Chinese systems to the Hindu place value system with zero.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: According to Reema's father, roughly how long ago did the Mesopotamian civilisation flourish in western Asia?
questions.explanation: The chapter opens with the father explaining that Mesopotamia (mostly present-day Iraq) flourished around 4000 years ago. 2000 years ago is when the ten-digit system developed in India, and 10,000 years ago is the Stone Age setting used later for counting cows.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Which ancient Indian text is named in the chapter for listing number names based on powers of 10 (eka, dasha, shata, sahasra...)?
questions.explanation: The Yajurveda Samhita listed names for one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand and so on, up to 10¹² and beyond. The other three are later works about computation and zero, not the source of these oral number names.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Where does the first known instance of writing numbers with ten digits, including a 0 written as a dot, occur?
questions.explanation: The Bakhshali manuscript (c. 3rd century CE) is the first known instance of all ten digits including a dot for zero. Aryabhata (499 CE) was the first to fully explain the system, and Brahmagupta (628 CE) codified zero as a number — both came later.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Which book by the Persian mathematician Al-Khwārizmī helped popularise the Indian numerals in the Arab world?
options: On the Use of the Hindu Numerals (c. 830)
On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals (c. 825)
questions.explanation: Al-Khwārizmī wrote 'On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals' around 825. 'On the Use of the Hindu Numerals' (c. 830) was by the philosopher Al-Kindi, an easy mix-up; the other two are Indian works.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: By about which year had the Hindu numerals reached Europe and parts of Africa from the Arab world?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives 1100 CE for transmission to Europe and Africa. 800 CE is when the Arab world received them, around 1200 Fibonacci argued for their adoption, and the 17th century is when Europe could no longer avoid them.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Why did European scholars call the Indian numerals 'Arabic numerals'?
options: Al-Kindi named them after his own homeland
Roman numerals were already called Hindu numerals
They had learned the numerals from Arab scholars
Arab scholars had invented the ten digit shapes
questions.explanation: Europeans learned the system from the Arab world, so the name reflected their own perspective. Arab scholars such as Al-Khwārizmī and Al-Kindi themselves called them 'Hindu numerals', crediting India.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: In the term 'Hindu numerals', what does the chapter say the word 'Hindu' refers to?
options: The religion that Aryabhata and Brahmagupta followed
The Latin title of Fibonacci's book on numbers
The geography and people the numbers came from
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly notes that 'Hindu' here does not refer to a religion but to a geography/people from whom the numerals came — the same sense in which Arab scholars used it.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Arab scholars such as Al-Khwārizmī and Al-Kindi referred to the numerals we use today as 'Hindu numerals'.
questions.explanation: Yes — the Arab scholars credited the source, calling them Hindu numerals; it was European scholars who later called them 'Arabic numerals'.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: After Fibonacci made the case for Indian numerals around 1200, Europe adopted them within a few decades.
questions.explanation: False. Roman numerals were so ingrained that the Indian numerals did not gain widespread use for several more centuries; only by the 17th century did not adopting them become impossible.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Pierre-Simon Laplace said that the Indian method of writing numbers with ten symbols 'placed arithmetic foremost among useful inventions'.
questions.explanation: The quotation from Laplace (1749–1827) praises the Indian system for the way it facilitated calculations and placed arithmetic foremost among useful inventions.

questions.topic: Origins and Spread of Hindu Numerals
questions.question: Select the TWO events that are correctly matched with their approximate dates in the chapter.
options: Aryabhata fully explains the ten-symbol system — c. 499 CE
Fibonacci urges Europe to adopt Indian numerals — c. 1200
Al-Khwārizmī writes his book on Hindu numerals — c. 1100
Indian numerals reach Europe and Africa — c. 800 CE
questions.explanation: Aryabhata (499 CE) and Fibonacci (c. 1200) are correct. Al-Khwārizmī's book was c. 825, not 1100, and the numerals reached Europe around 1100 CE, not 800 CE (800 CE is when they reached the Arab world).

questions.question: In Method 1, keeping one stick for every cow is called a one-to-one mapping. What does that mean?
options: Sticks are grouped into tens and ones
Each cow is matched to exactly one stick
Each stick stands for five cows at once
Cows are counted using letter sounds
questions.explanation: A one-to-one mapping associates each cow with its own stick so that no two cows share the same stick. The final pile of sticks then tells the size of the herd.

questions.question: What is the obvious limitation of counting with the sounds of the English letters a to z (Method 2)?
options: It cannot be spoken aloud, only written on surfaces
It groups objects in fives, which is hard to see
It cannot count collections of more than 26 objects
It needs as many letters as objects being counted
questions.explanation: There are only 26 letters, so a collection with more than 26 objects cannot be counted this way. Needing as many items as objects is the drawback of sticks, not letters.

questions.question: Using only sticks, how could you find how many MORE cows you need to equal your neighbour's herd (Q3)?
options: Count both piles aloud using letter names and subtract
Replace every five sticks with a notch and compare notches
Multiply your pile by the neighbour's pile of sticks
Pair your sticks with theirs; the unmatched sticks show the gap
questions.explanation: Match sticks one-to-one between the two piles. The sticks left over in the neighbour's pile with no partner show exactly how many cows you are short — no number names needed.

questions.question: The chapter calls a standard sequence of objects, names or symbols with a fixed order, used for counting, a:
questions.explanation: A number system is the standard fixed-order sequence we map objects onto when counting. A numeral is a written symbol within such a system; landmark numbers and bases are later refinements.

questions.question: Which statement about the three counting methods is NOT correct?
options: Method 3's symbols were used in Europe before the Hindu system
Roman symbols avoid the need for new symbols for very large numbers
Sticks give an unending sequence but are clumsy for big collections
Letter sounds are convenient but the sequence is not unending
questions.explanation: The Roman system (Method 3) had the drawback that one cannot write arbitrarily large numbers without introducing more and more symbols. The other three statements are exactly what the chapter says.

questions.question: Which group of people is mentioned as having all three forms of number representation — objects, names and written symbols?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that some groups had numbers as objects and names, while others like the Chinese had all three forms: physical objects, names and written symbols.

questions.question: Using only sticks (no number names), which procedure correctly SUBTRACTS one collection from another?
options: Remove as many sticks as the second collection, then count the rest
Put both collections together and count all the sticks
Make groups of equal numbers of sticks and count the groups
Lay sticks in rows equal to the second collection and count rows
questions.explanation: Subtraction with sticks means removing from the first collection a stick for each stick in the second, then counting the remainder. Putting together is addition; grouping equal piles is multiplication or division.

questions.question: The book's answer extends the letter system as a, b, ..., z, then aa, bb, cc, ... With a to z standing for 1 to 26 and 'aa' for 27, what does 'cc' stand for?
questions.explanation: aa = 27, bb = 28, cc = 29 — each doubled letter continues the sequence one at a time. 53 would be the wrong guess of 'c = 3, so cc = 26 + 27'.

questions.question: The symbols occurring in a written number system are called numerals.
questions.explanation: Numerals are the written symbols of a number system — for example 0, 1, 5, 36 and 193 are numerals of the Hindu number system.

questions.question: In this chapter, a 'number system' can only be made of written symbols, never of objects or spoken names.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter defines a number system as a standard sequence of objects, OR names, OR written symbols with a fixed order — sticks and letter sounds both count.

questions.question: Which TWO statements are true of the stick method (Method 1)?
options: It is an unending standard sequence
It needs as many sticks as there are objects
It can only count up to 26 objects
It is the system later called Roman numerals
questions.explanation: Sticks are unending (add one more) but inconvenient because you need one stick per object. The 26 limit belongs to letter sounds, and the Roman system is Method 3.

questions.question: What are tally marks, as described in the chapter?
options: Letters of an alphabet spoken in a fixed order
Knots tied on a rope, one for each animal counted
Notches cut on a surface such as a bone or cave wall
Pebbles arranged in rows of five on the ground
questions.explanation: Tally marks are notches — marks cut on a surface like a bone or a cave wall — with one mark made for each object counted.

questions.question: Which description matches the Lebombo bone?
options: Found in Congo, notches in columns, 20,000–35,000 years old
Found in Mesopotamia, wedge marks, about 4000 years old
Found in India, dot for zero, from the 3rd century CE
Found in South Africa, 29 notches, about 44,000 years old
questions.explanation: The Lebombo bone from South Africa has 29 notches and is about 44,000 years old — one of the oldest mathematical artefacts. The Congo description is the Ishango bone.

questions.question: Which statement about the ancient bones is NOT correct?
options: Bones with tally marks go back more than 20,000 years
The Lebombo bone has 29 notches and was found in Congo
The Lebombo bone is older than the Ishango bone
The Ishango bone's notches may indicate a calendar system
questions.explanation: The Lebombo bone was found in South Africa, not Congo (that is the Ishango bone). It is indeed older (≈44,000 vs 20,000–35,000 years), and the Ishango notches in columns possibly indicate calendars.

questions.question: How does the tally-mark method differ from the stick method of counting?
options: Tally marks can count only up to 26 objects
Sticks map one-to-one but tally marks do not
A mark is cut for each object instead of adding a stick
Marks are grouped by landmark numbers but sticks are not
questions.explanation: The chapter says tally marking is very similar to using sticks — one mark per object — except that a mark is made instead of adding a stick. Both are one-to-one mappings.

questions.question: The chapter describes a group of people who used (and still use) their body parts as their number system. Where do they live?
questions.explanation: A group of people in Papua New Guinea used and still use their hands and other body parts as a standard sequence for counting.

questions.question: The Ishango bone is older than the Lebombo bone.
questions.explanation: False. The Lebombo bone (≈44,000 years) is described as 'an even older tally stick' than the Ishango bone (20,000–35,000 years).

questions.question: The 29 notches on the Lebombo bone may have served as a lunar calendar.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Lebombo bone may have served as a tally stick or a lunar calendar.

questions.question: In the Gumulgal number system, urapon = 1 and ukasar = 2. What number is 'ukasar-ukasar-urapon'?
questions.explanation: ukasar-ukasar-urapon = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. The Gumulgal counted in twos and built names by adding twos and a possible one.

questions.question: What did the Gumulgal call any number greater than 6?
questions.explanation: The Gumulgal had names only up to 6 (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar); any number greater than 6 was simply called 'ras'. 'ahage' is a Bakairi word for 2.

questions.question: How do historians explain that the Gumulgal (Australia), Bakairi (South America) and Bushmen (South Africa) have equivalent number systems?
options: They may share common ancestors who used this system
Traders carried the system between the three continents
Counting in twos is the only system humans can invent
The Romans spread their system of fives to all three
questions.explanation: The groups are far apart with no trace of contact, so one theory is that they had common ancestors who used the system, and their descendants migrated to these places.

questions.question: Which of these group sizes is NOT listed in the chapter as a commonly used group size in number systems?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists 2, 5, 10 and 20 as commonly used group sizes. Seven is not among them (base-7 appears only as an exercise to compute landmark numbers).

questions.question: Most humans find it difficult to know the size of a group at a single glance when it has:
questions.explanation: The chapter's activity concludes that most humans find it difficult to count groups having 5 or more objects in a single glance — a perceptual limit.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what might have prompted people to replace every group of five tally marks with a new symbol?
options: Bones were too small to hold more than five notches
Five is the number of landmark numbers in a base system
Trade laws required goods to be counted in fives
Our limit of perceiving about five objects at a glance
questions.explanation: The human limit for immediately recognising the size of a collection (about 5) could have led tally users to replace each group of 5 marks with a new symbol — the idea seen in Roman V.

questions.question: If a system counts ONLY in groups of 5, how many groups of 5 are needed to represent 1345?
questions.explanation: 1345 ÷ 5 = 269 exactly. Writing a symbol 269 times shows why counting in a single group size becomes cumbersome for larger numbers.

questions.question: In the Gumulgal system (urapon = 1, ukasar = 2), what is (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon)?
questions.explanation: The numbers are 9 and 7; 9 + 7 = 16 = 2 × 8, so the sum is eight ukasars. Note that the two urapons combine into one extra ukasar — forgetting this gives 7 ukasars + urapon.

questions.question: In the Gumulgal system, (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) − (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) equals:
questions.explanation: 9 − 6 = 3 = 2 + 1 = ukasar-urapon. Removing three ukasars from four ukasars and an urapon leaves one ukasar and one urapon.

questions.question: In the Gumulgal system, (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) × (ukasar-ukasar) is:
questions.explanation: 9 × 2 = 18, and 18 = 2 × 9, so the product is nine ukasars. Writing ukasar 18 times would be 36 — a common slip of counting ones instead of twos.

questions.question: In the Gumulgal system, (ukasar repeated 8 times) ÷ (ukasar-ukasar) equals:
questions.explanation: Eight ukasars = 16 and ukasar-ukasar = 4; 16 ÷ 4 = 4 = 2 + 2 = ukasar-ukasar. The tempting 'four ukasars' (8) comes from dividing by ukasar (2) instead of by ukasar-ukasar (4).

questions.question: The Gumulgal had distinct number names for numbers up to 10.
questions.explanation: False. Gumulgal names went only up to 6 (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar); anything greater than 6 was called 'ras'.

questions.question: Using the Roman grouping into 10s, then 5s, then 1s, how is 27 written?
questions.explanation: 27 = 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, so it is XXVII. XXVI is 26; the other two do not follow the rule of taking as many 10s, then 5s, then 1s as possible.

questions.question: Which Roman symbol stands for 500?
questions.explanation: The landmark numbers are I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500 and M=1000. D is 500; L is 50, C is 100 and M is 1000.

questions.question: Following the pattern that 4 is written IV (1 less than 5), 40 is written as:
questions.explanation: 40 is 10 less than 50, so it is XL (X before L). LX would be 60. The chapter notes people were not always consistent and sometimes wrote XXXX.

questions.question: Writing 2367 as 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1, which Roman numeral results?
questions.explanation: Two Ms, three Cs, one L, one X, one V and two Is give MMCCCLXVII. MMCCCLXII (missing the V) would be 2362, MMCCLXVII is 2267 and MMMCCLXVII is 3267.

questions.question: What is 2999 in Roman numerals?
questions.explanation: 2999 = 2000 (MM) + 900 (CM) + 90 (XC) + 9 (IX) = MMCMXCIX. MMMCMXCIX is 3999, MMCMXIX is 2919, and 'VIX' is not a valid grouping.

questions.question: What is 715 in Roman numerals?
questions.explanation: 715 = 500 (D) + 100 + 100 (CC) + 10 (X) + 5 (V) = DCCXV. DCCXIV is 714, CCCXV is 315, and 'VX' is not a valid grouping.

questions.question: The Roman number system seems to have evolved from which earlier system, and roughly when?
options: The Hindu system, around the 3rd century CE
The ancient Greek system, around the 8th century BCE
The Egyptian system, around 3000 BCE in Egypt
The Mesopotamian system, about 4000 years ago
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Roman system seems to have evolved out of the ancient Greek number system in around the 8th century BCE in Rome, spreading with the Roman empire.

questions.question: What number does the Roman numeral XLIV represent?
questions.explanation: XL = 40 (10 less than 50) and IV = 4 (1 less than 5), so XLIV = 44. Reading XL as 60 (LX) gives the wrong 64 or 66.

questions.question: The chapter calls numbers with their own basic symbol 'landmark numbers'. Which of these is NOT a Roman landmark number?
questions.explanation: The Roman landmark numbers listed are 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500 and 1000. There is no basic symbol for 5000, which is exactly why very large numbers are hard to write in this system.

questions.question: In the Roman system, 50 is normally written as XXXXX.
questions.explanation: False. Instead of XXXXX, a new symbol L was given to 50. (40, however, was sometimes written as XXXX.)

questions.question: Roman numerals spread throughout Europe with the expansion of the Roman empire.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the system spread throughout Europe with the expansion of the Roman empire and was used for centuries.

questions.question: Adding CCXXXII + CCCCXIII without converting, you collect 6 Cs, 4 Xs and 5 Is. Why does the chapter regroup the Cs?
options: Because five Cs (100s) make a D (500)
Because a C can never be repeated twice
Because six Cs must be written as DC·C
Because Cs and Xs must be added separately
questions.explanation: Six Cs are 600; five of them are regrouped as D (500), leaving DC. The whole sum is 232 + 413 = 645 = DCXLV.

questions.question: LXXXVII + LXXVIII equals which Roman numeral?
questions.explanation: 87 + 78 = 165 = 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 = CLXV. Directly: two Ls make a C, the five Xs make an L, VV = X, and the five Is make a V.

questions.question: The product of the landmark numbers V × L is:
questions.explanation: 5 × 50 = 250 = 100 + 100 + 50 = CCL. Notice the product of two landmark numbers is NOT itself a landmark number here — unlike in a base system.

questions.question: L × D would be written as M repeated 25 times. What is this product in Hindu numerals?
questions.explanation: 50 × 500 = 25,000. Since the largest symbol is M (1000), one needs 25 Ms — a vivid example of why Roman multiplication and large numbers are awkward.

questions.question: VII × IX in Roman numerals is:
questions.explanation: 7 × 9 = 63 = 50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 = LXIII. LXVIII is 68 and XLIII is 43.

questions.question: CCXXXI × MDCCCLII equals which number?
questions.explanation: CCXXXI = 231 and MDCCCLII = 1852. 231 × 1852 = 231,000 + 184,800 + 12,012 = 427,812. The distractors come from slips in one partial product.

questions.question: Why is multiplication hard in the Roman system, according to the chapter?
options: Landmark × landmark need not give another landmark number
Roman numerals cannot represent any even numbers
There is no symbol for 100 or 1000 in the system
Only numbers below 39 can be multiplied together
questions.explanation: In a base system landmark × landmark gives another landmark (10 × 100 = 1000), but in the Roman system V × L = 250 has no single symbol, so multiplication needs messy regrouping.

questions.question: Which calculating tool did people using the Roman system rely on for arithmetic?
questions.explanation: People using Roman numerals used a calculating tool called the abacus, though only specially trained people could use it.

questions.question: The chapter says each number system in history developed as a direct improvement on the previous one.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter warns that it should NOT be understood that one system historically developed as an improvement over the previous one; the real story is much more complex.

questions.question: Which TWO features of the Hindu number system make it more efficient than Roman numerals, per the book's answer?
options: It is a place value system
It has a symbol and concept for zero
It has more landmark symbols than the Roman system
It uses letters of the alphabet as its digits
questions.explanation: The book's comparison lists place value, the concept of zero, and ease of calculation for the Hindu system versus fixed values, no zero and difficult calculation for Roman numerals. More symbols or letter-digits are not advantages.

questions.question: Around when did the Egyptians develop the written number system described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The Egyptian system dates from around 3000 BCE. 200 BCE is when the Hindu system had a symbol for zero, and 800 CE is when the Indian numerals reached the Arab world.

questions.question: What is special about the sequence of landmark numbers in the Egyptian system?
options: Each landmark number is 5 more than the previous one
Each landmark number is 60 times the previous one
Each landmark number is 10 times the previous one
questions.explanation: Starting from 1, each Egyptian landmark number is 10 times the previous — 1, 10, 100, 1000... — so they are all powers of 10. Alternating 5s and 10s is the Roman pattern; 60 is Mesopotamian.

questions.question: 324 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 ones. How many symbols in total does the Egyptian numeral for 324 use?
questions.explanation: Three hundred-symbols + two ten-symbols + four one-strokes = 9 symbols. The Hindu numeral needs just 3 digits, but the Egyptian numeral repeats each symbol as many times as needed.

questions.question: In the Egyptian numeral for 10458 (= 10000 + 400 + 50 + 8), which landmark symbol does NOT appear at all?
questions.explanation: 10458 has one 10000, four 100s, five 10s and eight 1s — there is no 1000 in the grouping, so that symbol is simply absent (a blank the Egyptians never needed to mark).

questions.question: How many symbols are needed to write 70707 in the Egyptian system?
questions.explanation: 70707 = 7 × 10000 + 7 × 100 + 7 × 1, so seven 10000-symbols, seven 100-symbols and seven 1-strokes: 21 symbols. There are no 1000s or 10s.

questions.question: Which of these numbers needs the FEWEST symbols when written in the Egyptian system?
questions.explanation: 1111 uses one symbol of each kind: 4 symbols. 1023 needs 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, 2660 needs 14 and 784 needs 7 + 8 + 4 = 19. The size of a number does not decide its symbol count — its digits do.

questions.question: Can an Egyptian numeral contain the same symbol 10 or more times? Why?
options: Yes — but only the one-stroke symbol may appear ten or more times
No — ten of any landmark symbol are regrouped as the next landmark
Yes — any symbol may be repeated as often as a scribe needs
No — scribes were only allowed to carve five of a symbol
questions.explanation: Since 10 times any landmark number gives the next landmark number, ten copies of a symbol are always replaced by one symbol of the next landmark. So each symbol appears at most 9 times.

questions.question: What was the main shortcoming of the Egyptian system noted in the chapter?
options: Addition required converting to Roman numerals first
It had no fixed order for writing its landmark symbols
Ever larger numbers needed an unending supply of new symbols
It could not represent any number greater than one hundred
questions.explanation: The Egyptian system worked well up to a crore (10⁷), but representing larger and larger numbers required inventing new symbols for higher and higher powers of 10 — the original challenge resurfacing.

questions.question: Up to roughly what size did the Egyptian system give relatively efficient number representations?
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Egyptian system enabled relatively efficient representation for numbers till a crore (10⁷) before new symbols would be required.

questions.question: The Egyptian number system is a base-10 (decimal) system.
questions.explanation: Yes — its landmark numbers are 1, 10, 100, 1000, ..., all powers of 10, so it is base-10, also called decimal.

questions.question: In the Egyptian system, the position where a symbol is written decides which power of 10 it stands for.
questions.explanation: False. Each Egyptian landmark number had its own distinct symbol, so meaning did not depend on position. Position-based meaning is the later idea of place value (Mesopotamian, Mayan, Chinese, Hindu).

questions.question: A number system is called base-n when its first landmark number is 1 and every next landmark number is obtained by:
options: multiplying the current landmark number by a fixed number n
adding the fixed number n to the current landmark number
doubling the current landmark number n times
writing the current landmark number n positions to the left
questions.explanation: In a base-n system each landmark number is n times the previous one, so the landmark numbers are 1, n, n², n³, ... — the powers of n.

questions.question: In the base-5 system created in the chapter, what is the fourth landmark number?
questions.explanation: The landmark numbers are 5⁰ = 1, 5¹ = 5, 5² = 25, 5³ = 125, 5⁴ = 625. Counting from 1 as the first, the fourth is 125.

questions.question: Which grouping of 143 is the correct one for the base-5 system (where 5 of a landmark must be regrouped)?
questions.explanation: 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1. 'Five 25s' and 'eight 1s' also add to 143 but are invalid — five 25s must become one 125 and five 1s must become a 5. 'One 125, one 25, three 1s' is 153.

questions.question: How many symbols in total are needed to write 293 in the chapter's base-5 system?
Is there a number that cannot be represented in the chapter's base-5 system? The book's answer is:
options: Yes — numbers above 3125, as there is no larger symbol
Yes — any number with 5 or more of one landmark
Yes — zero, because the system has no symbol for it
No — every whole number can be grouped into powers of 5
questions.explanation: The book answers that zero cannot be represented since there is no symbol for 'nothing'. Numbers above 3125 would just need a new landmark symbol, and 5 of a landmark can always be regrouped.

questions.question: Which of these is a landmark number of a base-7 system?
questions.explanation: Base-7 landmark numbers are 7⁰ = 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ... 343 = 7³. 243 is 3⁵, a tempting near-miss.

questions.question: A base-10 number system is also called a:
questions.explanation: Base-10 is called the decimal system. Sexagesimal means base-60 (Mesopotamian), and positional refers to place value, which base-10 systems like the Egyptian one need not have.

questions.question: Which statement about base-n systems is NOT true?
options: The landmark numbers of a base-n system are the powers of n
The landmark numbers of base-5 include 5, 10, 15 and 20
In base-n, each landmark number is n times the previous one
The first landmark number of every base-n system is 1
questions.explanation: Base-5 landmark numbers are powers of 5 (1, 5, 25, 125...), not multiples of 5. The other three statements are the chapter's definition.

questions.question: The book's own base-4 system uses ∟ for 1, ∆ for 4 and □ for 16. How is 11 written?
questions.explanation: 11 = 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 → two ∆ and three ∟. ∆∆∆∟∟ is 14, □∟∟∟ is 19, and seven ∟ should be regrouped (four ∟ = ∆).

questions.question: Which TWO of these numbers are landmark numbers of a base-4 system?
questions.explanation: Base-4 landmark numbers are 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 — the powers of 4. 8, 12 and 24 are multiples of 4 but not powers of 4.

questions.question: Adding two Egyptian numerals gives 15 ten-symbols and 15 one-strokes. After regrouping, what number is the sum?
questions.explanation: 15 ones = 1 ten + 5 ones; now 16 tens = 1 hundred + 6 tens. Result: 1 hundred, 6 tens, 5 ones = 165 (which is just 150 + 15).

questions.question: Why is addition in a base-n system simpler than in the Roman system?
options: Roman numerals have more symbols to keep track of
Base systems write numbers with far fewer symbols
Every landmark regroups by the same size n into the next
Base systems never need any regrouping at all
questions.explanation: In the Roman system the grouping size changes (5 Is → V, but only 2 Vs → X), so regrouping needs care. In a base-n system every landmark regroups by the same n, making the process uniform.

questions.question: On the abacus board described in the chapter, what did a counter placed ABOVE a line contribute?
options: A value of 5 of that line's power of 10
A value of 10 of that line's power of 10
A value of 1, like a counter on the line
Nothing — it marked a blank position
questions.explanation: Each line stood for a power of 10, and a counter above a line contributed a value of 5 (of that power). This is how the 6 ones in 3426 were shown: one counter above (5) and one on the line (1).

questions.question: On the abacus, 3426 shows its 6 ones using how many counters on the units line?
options: Three counters above the line (2 each)
Two: one above the line (5) and one on it (1)
Six separate counters placed on the line
One counter above the line, standing for all 6
questions.explanation: Because a counter above the line is worth 5, six ones need just one counter above (5) plus one on the line (1) — two counters instead of six.

questions.question: Using the abacus for 2907 + 43, the 7 ones and 3 ones make 10. What is the final sum?
questions.explanation: 7 + 3 = 10 ones, which become one counter on the tens line; 0 + 4 + 1 = 5 tens. The total is 2950.

questions.question: What is a simple rule for multiplying a number by 5 in the chapter's base-5 system?
options: Write the whole number five times in a row
Add a one-symbol at the end of the number
Replace each symbol by five copies of itself
Shift each symbol to the symbol of the next landmark
questions.explanation: Multiplying by the base turns each landmark into the next (1→5, 5→25, 25→125), so every symbol simply shifts up one landmark — exactly like the Egyptian rule for multiplying by 10.

questions.question: In the chapter's base-5 system, 5 times a landmark number gives the next landmark number.
questions.explanation: Yes — the chapter reminds us of this while adding base-5 numerals: five copies of a symbol regroup into one of the next landmark.

questions.question: In the Roman system, the product of two landmark numbers is always another landmark number.
questions.explanation: False. For example V × L = 250 and V × D = 2500 have no single Roman symbol. This only holds when landmark numbers are powers of one base.

questions.question: Which TWO properties make a base-n system efficient for arithmetic, according to the chapter?
options: The product of two landmark numbers is another landmark number
Every landmark regroups into the next by the same size n
The position of a symbol decides its value
Only one symbol is ever needed for all numbers
questions.explanation: Uniform regrouping makes addition simple and landmark products being landmarks makes multiplication simple. Position-based value is place value (a separate later idea), and no system uses just one symbol.

questions.question: The Mesopotamian base-60 system is also called the:
questions.explanation: Base-60 is the sexagesimal system (also known as the Babylonian system). Decimal is base-10; 'positional' describes place value in general.

questions.question: Where can the influence of the Mesopotamian sexagesimal system still be seen today?
options: 100 paise in a rupee and 100 cm in a metre
360 degrees in a full turn of a wheel
12 months in a year and 7 days in a week
questions.explanation: The chapter points to our units of time — 60 minutes in an hour, 60 seconds in a minute — as a surviving trace of base 60.

questions.question: Grouping 640 into Mesopotamian landmark numbers gives:
questions.explanation: 640 = 10 × 60 + 40: ten 60s and one 40. The compact representation reads 'ten 60s and one 40', dropping the Egyptian-style ten separate 60-symbols.

questions.question: The expression (1) × 3600 + (70) × 60 + 2 must be regrouped because no power of 60 may occur 60 or more times. What number is it?
questions.explanation: 70 sixties = 60 sixties + 10 sixties = one 3600 + 10 sixties. So it becomes (2) × 3600 + (10) × 60 + 2 = 7200 + 600 + 2 = 7802.

questions.question: How is 200 grouped for the Mesopotamian system?
questions.explanation: 200 = 3 × 60 + 20. Writing 2 × 60 + 80 is invalid because 80 ones exceed 59 and must be regrouped.

questions.question: Among 63, 132, 200 and 3605, which needs a BLANK (or placeholder) in its Mesopotamian representation?
questions.explanation: 3605 = 1 × 3600 + 0 × 60 + 5 — the 60s position is empty and needs a blank or placeholder. 63 = 1×60+3, 132 = 2×60+12 and 200 = 3×60+20 have no empty position.

questions.question: Why can the Mesopotamian system NOT be considered a fully developed place value system?
options: Its numerals were written from bottom to top
Inconsistent blank spacing, and no placeholder at the end
It had no landmark numbers and relied only on tally marks
It used a different symbol for every power of 60
questions.explanation: Spacing for blanks varied between scribes, causing ambiguity, and even the later placeholder symbol was used mainly in the middle of numbers, not at the end — so 60 and 3600 could look alike.

questions.question: A number system with a base that uses the POSITION of each symbol to determine its landmark number is called a:
questions.explanation: Such a system is called a positional or place value system — the Mesopotamian system is the chapter's first example. Sexagesimal only means base-60.

questions.question: The later Mesopotamians used their placeholder symbol mainly at the end of numbers, such as for 3600.
questions.explanation: False. The placeholder was primarily used in the middle of numbers, not at the end, so a number like 3600 still remained ambiguous.

questions.question: Using only the symbols for 1 and 10, the Mesopotamians could write every number from 1 to 59.
questions.explanation: Yes — combinations of the wedge for 1 and the hook for 10 express 1 to 59, and these groups are then placed in positions for each power of 60.

questions.question: Which TWO are theories the chapter mentions for why the Mesopotamians chose base 60?
options: A link to periods of important events, like the 30-day lunar month
Sixty is the total of fingers and toes of three people
The Egyptians had already been using base 60
questions.explanation: The chapter lists connections with periods of events (lunar month, Sun's apparent revolution), ease of fractions, and their earlier landmark sequence collapsing to powers of 60. Egypt used base 10, and the finger-toe idea is not in the chapter.

questions.question: The Mayan civilisation, which designed its own place value system, flourished in:
options: Central America, between the 3rd and 10th centuries CE
South America, between the 8th and 3rd centuries BCE
Western Asia, about 4000 years ago, in Mesopotamia
Central America, around the 17th century CE
questions.explanation: The Mayans made great intellectual progress in Central America between the 3rd and 10th centuries CE, designing a place value system independently of Asia.

questions.question: What did the Mayan placeholder symbol for zero look like?
questions.explanation: The Mayan zero looked like a seashell. A dot stood for 1 and a bar for 5; the wedge belongs to the Mesopotamian system.

questions.question: In Mayan notation (dot = 1, bar = 5), how is 17 written?
questions.explanation: 17 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 2, so three bars and two dots. Five dots would always be regrouped into a bar, so 7 or 12 dots is invalid.

questions.question: What are the first three Mayan landmark numbers given in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The Mayan landmark numbers were 1, 20 and then 360 — not 400 as a true base-20 would give, which puzzles scholars and may relate to their calendar.

questions.question: In the Mayan representation of 721, which grouping is used?
questions.explanation: 721 = 720 + 1 = 2 × 360 + 0 × 20 + 1, so the 20s position holds a seashell zero. '36 twenties' is invalid (a position holds at most 19), and 1 × 360 + 18 × 20 also equals 720 but 18 twenties = 360 must be regrouped into a second 360. (2)×360 + (1)×20 + 1 is 741.

questions.question: Why does the Mayan system lack the computational advantages of a base system?
options: Its numbers were written vertically instead of horizontally
Its third landmark is 360, so it is not a true base-20 system
It had no placeholder symbol for an empty position
It used only two different symbols, a dot and a bar for five
questions.explanation: Because 360 is not 20², the landmark numbers are not all powers of one base, so landmark products are not landmarks and the base advantages are lost. The dot/bar and vertical writing are not the problem.

questions.question: In the Mayan vertical layout, which set of symbols is written LOWEST?
options: The set showing the number of 360s
The set showing the number of 1s
The set showing the number of 20s
questions.explanation: Symbols were stacked with the lowest set for the 1s, the set above it for the 20s, and the set above that for the 360s.

questions.question: The Chinese rod numerals were a decimal system developed by at least the 3rd century AD and used until the:
questions.explanation: Rod numerals developed in China by at least the 3rd century AD and were used till the 17th century.

questions.question: In the rod numeral for 2634, which positions use the zong (vertical) form of the digits?
questions.explanation: Zongs represent units, hundreds, tens of thousands...; hengs represent tens, thousands, hundreds of thousands. So 2634 reads 2 (heng), 6 (zong), 3 (heng), 4 (zong).

questions.question: If only zong rods were used with no clear spacing, 41 would appear as five rods in a row. Which reading is IMPOSSIBLE for that numeral?
questions.explanation: Five rods could be split as 4|1, 2|3, 3|2 or 1|2|2 and so on — but 33 would need six rods. Alternating zong and heng avoids this ambiguity between adjacent places.

questions.question: The Mayan number system is a true base-20 system.
questions.explanation: False. Its landmark numbers go 1, 20, 360 — the third is not 20² = 400 — so the chapter says it is not an actual base-20 system.

questions.question: Which TWO of these numbers need a seashell (zero) in the 20s position when written in the Mayan system?
questions.explanation: 361 = 1×360 + 0×20 + 1 and 721 = 2×360 + 0×20 + 1 both have an empty 20s position. 77 = 3×20 + 17 has no zero, and 100 = 5×20 + 0 has its zero in the UNITS position.

questions.question: The Hindu number system has had a symbol for zero since at least:
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Hindu system had a symbol for 0 at least as early as 200 BCE. 499 CE and 628 CE are the dates of Aryabhata's and Brahmagupta's works, and the Bakhshali manuscript is 3rd century CE.

questions.question: In the Hindu system the numeral 375 is read as:
questions.explanation: 375 = 3 hundreds + 7 tens + 5 ones. Position decides the power of 10: the rightmost digit counts 1s, then 10s, then 100s.

questions.question: Which mathematician explicitly used the properties '0 + any number = that number' and '0 × any number = 0' in computations in 499 CE?
options: Fibonacci, in his arguments to Europe
Al-Khwārizmī, in his book on Hindu numerals
questions.explanation: Aryabhata used these arithmetic properties of zero in the Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE). Brahmagupta (628 CE) later codified zero as a number in its own right.

questions.question: Who codified the use of 0 as a number on which arithmetic operations can be performed, and in which work?
options: Al-Kindi, On the Use of the Hindu Numerals (c. 830)
Laplace, in his praise of the Indian system
questions.explanation: Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) codified zero as a number like any other. Aryabhata used zero's properties earlier but the codification is credited to Brahmagupta.

questions.question: The chapter says Brahmagupta's numbers formed a 'ring'. Which operation is NOT part of the closure that defines a ring here?
questions.explanation: A ring is a set closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication — any two numbers combined by these give another number in the set. Division is not included (e.g. 1 ÷ 2 is not a whole number).

questions.question: Why does the Hindu system avoid the ambiguities of the Mesopotamian system?
options: It uses 0 as a digit and exactly one digit in each position
It uses a larger base, so fewer positions are needed
It writes numbers vertically so positions cannot merge
It gives every power of 10 its own distinct symbol
questions.explanation: Zero as a digit removes blank-space confusion, and a single digit per position means every position is clearly marked. Distinct symbols per power is the Egyptian approach, not the Hindu one.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the five ideas in the 'Evolution of Ideas in Number Representation' box?
options: place value → base → landmark numbers → groups → zero
groups → landmark numbers → base → place value → zero
landmark numbers → groups → base → zero → place value
groups → base → landmark numbers → place value → zero
questions.explanation: The box lists: (1) count in groups of a single number, (2) group using landmark numbers, (3) choose powers of a number as landmarks — a base, (4) use positions — place value, (5) 0 as a digit and a number.

questions.question: Which statement about the Hindu number system is NOT correct?
options: It writes all numbers with just ten symbols
Zero is treated on par with the other digits
It is a place value system with base 10
It needs a new symbol for each higher power of 10
questions.explanation: The whole point of place value is that NO new symbols are needed for higher powers — positions carry that information. Needing a new symbol per power was the Egyptian shortcoming.

questions.question: The Hindu number system is a place value system with ten digits, in which 0 is treated on par with the other digits.
questions.explanation: Yes — the summary describes it as a place value system with (usually) 10 digits including 0, which is treated on par with the other digits.

questions.question: Indian mathematicians used zero only as a placeholder and never treated it as a number in its own right.
questions.explanation: False. In Indian mathematics zero was given the status of a number on par with others — Aryabhata used its arithmetic properties and Brahmagupta codified operations with it.

questions.question: Which TWO of these civilisations used place value representations, according to the summary?
questions.explanation: Place value was used by the Mesopotamian (Babylonian), Mayan, Chinese and Indian civilisations. The Egyptian and Roman systems used distinct symbols for landmark numbers without positional meaning.

questions.question: Writing the base-10 numeral 25 in base-8 (as the book does) gives:
questions.explanation: 25 = 3 × 8 + 1, so the base-8 digits are 3 and 1: '31'. Reading it as thirty-one is a slip — in base-8 '31' means three 8s and one 1.

questions.question: Writing the base-10 numeral 25 in base-5 gives:
questions.explanation: 25 = 1 × 5² + 0 × 5 + 0 × 1, so it is written '100' in base-5 — one 25, no 5s, no 1s. Each 0 is a placeholder digit.

questions.question: Writing the base-10 numeral 25 in base-2 gives:
In the book's base-2 place value system with urapon = 0 and ukasar = 1, what number is 'uk uk ur'?
questions.explanation: uk uk ur = 1×2² + 1×2¹ + 0×2⁰ = 4 + 2 + 0 = 6. Compare the Gumulgal 'ukasar-ukasar-urapon', which means 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 — same words, different system!

questions.question: Which of these cannot be a digit in a base-8 Hindu-style numeral?
questions.explanation: In base-8 the digits run from 0 to 7 (0 ≤ aᵢ ≤ 7 in the book's formula). Eight of anything is regrouped into the next position, so 8 itself is never a digit.

questions.question: If humans had 8 fingers and used base-8, the landmark numbers would be:
questions.explanation: Landmark numbers are the powers of the base: 8⁰ = 1, 8¹ = 8, 8² = 64, 8³ = 512. Multiples of 8 (16, 24) are not powers, and 0 is never a landmark number.

questions.question: Using the same method as the book, the base-10 number 41 written as a base-5 Hindu-style numeral is:
Using the book's base-8 method, what base-10 number does the base-8 numeral '123' represent?
questions.explanation: '123' in base-8 = 1 × 64 + 2 × 8 + 3 × 1 = 64 + 16 + 3 = 83. Reading it as one hundred twenty-three ignores that the places are powers of 8.

questions.question: Why does the chapter suggest the ancient Indians likely chose base 10?
options: Ten is the smallest number with a symbol for zero
The Egyptians had already fixed base 10
Ten is the number of letters in 'Yajurveda'
Humans have 10 fingers to count on
questions.explanation: The chapter says base 10 was likely chosen because humans have 10 fingers and so can count on them — which is why it asks what we would do with 8 fingers.

questions.question: 25 written in base-8 is '31' because 25 = 3 × 8 + 1.
questions.explanation: Yes — three 8s and one 1 give the base-8 digits 3 and 1, so 25 (base-10) = 31 (base-8).

questions.question: In the book's base-2 system, 'uk ur' means 2, and in the Gumulgal system 'ukasar-urapon' means 2 as well.
questions.explanation: False. In base-2, uk ur = 1×2 + 0 = 2, but in the Gumulgal system ukasar-urapon = 2 + 1 = 3. Same words, different systems — the book's table contrasts exactly this.

questions.question: Which TWO of these numbers need FEWER than 10 symbols when written in the Egyptian system?
questions.explanation: 1023 needs 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 symbols and 1111 needs 4. But 784 needs 7 + 8 + 4 = 19, 2660 needs 14 and 70707 needs 21 — the count depends on the digits, not on the size of the number.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about the Mesopotamian system are correct?
options: Numbers from 1 to 59 were built from just the symbols for 1 and 10
A blank space showed that a power of 60 did not occur
It was a base-10 system like the Egyptian system
Its placeholder symbol was always written at the end of numbers
questions.explanation: The wedge (1) and hook (10) build 1–59, and a blank marked an empty position for a power of 60. The system was base-60, not base-10, and the later placeholder was used mainly in the middle of numbers, not at the end.

questions.question: Select the TWO correct ways of writing the base-10 number 25 in another base.
